CAPTA: Identifying LLMs Behind AI Agents

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (202 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.32686v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents access remote services through tools to complete user tasks, often via API calls. In this setting, a remote service may want to identify the backend LLM of an agent to launch model-specific attacks, including prompt injection or selective delivery of manipulated content. However, the service cannot directly query the backend model and must instead collect observable responses through its interactions with the agent, making identification challenging. In this paper, we present Completely Automated Preference Test to tell LLMs Apart (CAPTA), a model identification approach inspired by CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), which distinguishes humans from automated programs. CAPTA presents multiple-choice questions as verification challenges, using differences in models' selection preferences to identify the backend LLM. It selects questions based on cross-model option-generation diversity and uses LLM-guided search to optimize their option sets. Our evaluation highlights that CAPTA achieves 99.0% mean identification accuracy with only 10 questions across 25 LLMs from 10 model families. We further evaluate CAPTA with four widely used agents and seven representative LLMs, achieving 99.7% mean identification accuracy across all 28 agent-LLM combinations with 30 submitted answers.

Breaking: How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?

📅 18 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and demonstrated that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs.
  • Sources indicate that equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance.
  • It has been revealed that agentic memory is not a feature you switch on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and demonstrated that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs. the whole set injected — drives both accuracy and cost. This post steps back to the question that comes before it: how much should you give it?

Sources indicate that equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance. It doesn't always work that way. When we scaled the evaluation to eight models — from a 30B dense model to frontier proprietary systems — one finding stood out:.

It has been revealed that agentic memory is not a feature you switch on. It's a dose you calibrate to the model.

ALTK-Evolve lets an agent learn from its own past trajectories: distilling reusable guidelines and injecting them back at inference time, with no weight updates and no human annotation.

The right dose differs by model tier: strong models with headroom want the full guideline set, weaker models do best with a compact core plus per-task retrieval, and saturated models show no measurable gain.

Curated retrieval can be both the most accurate and the cheapest option: gpt-oss-120b gained +16.1pp task completion at only +5% tokens — and prompt caching keeps even the full guideline set affordable in production.

Sources indicate that not every model benefits from the same amount of memory. Across eight models spanning the capability spectrum, we saw three recurring patterns:.

Strong models with headroom want the full guideline set — every guideline, including rare edge-case lessons. They have the capacity to absorb and apply all of it. DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B MoE) climbed +9.5 percentage points in task completion when given its full self-mined guideline set.

Sources indicate that smaller or weaker models get drowned by a large guideline set. For these, a tight, high-confidence core plus a handful of task-relevant guidelines retrieved per task works best. gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE) gained +16.1pp with this selective approach — while the full guideline set gained less and cost ~50% more tokens.

According to recent reports, already-saturated models show no measurable gain. We call this the saturated pattern — the label describes what we observed, not a proven cause. The model may already have been near its ceiling on these tasks, the guidelines may not have addressed its remaining failures, or it may not have applied the guidance effectively. GLM-5 (745B MoE) sat here in our runs.

What puts a model into one pattern rather than another isn't simply parameter count. Benchmark headroom, context-window size, architecture, guideline quality, and task distribution all appear to shape where a model lands, and separating those factors is ongoing work. The practical takeaway holds either way: the right dose of memory depends on the model, and we can calibrate it.

"Memory" here doesn't mean replaying a past transcript. It means a guideline set — strategies that worked, mistakes to avoid, and edge cases — distilled from the agent's own prior trajectories. The loop is straightforward:.

The agent attempts tasks and produces trajectories.

ALTK-Evolve extracts behavioral guidelines from both its successful and unsuccessful runs.

It consolidates those guidelines into a reusable set.

At inference time, the agent receives either the full guideline set or a task-relevant selection of it.

Sources indicate that no model weights are updated. The learning loop changes the guidance available to the agent, not the underlying model — which is exactly why it's cheap to adopt and portable across the eight models we tested.

We evaluated on AppWorld — 585 multi-step tasks (168 test_normal + 417 test_challenge) across 9 simulated apps (calendars, messaging, payments, and so on). Tasks are scored two ways: whether the agent fully completes each task (TGC — Task Goal Completion) and whether every variant of a scenario passes (SGC — Scenario Goal Completion, a stricter, all-or-nothing bar). Full definitions are in the appendix.

Because the confusing part of any memory study is what's actually in the context window, we define the configurations up front.

It has been revealed that both memory configurations draw from the same guideline set, mined once (via the loop above) from AppWorld's training split only. What changes between them is only how that one set is delivered — the full guideline set injects all of it every step, while curated retrieval delivers a selected subset — never how the guidelines were produced, and no test-split data ever goes into building it.

It has been revealed that the number of guidelines a model mines depends on its own capability, so we report configurations by strategy — "full guideline set" vs. "curated retrieval" — rather than by raw counts, which aren't comparable across models.

Representative models from the eight-model sweep, measured by task completion (TGC) on test_normal:.

Figure 1. Representative models in the three observed patterns. Bars show TGC on AppWorld test_normal for baseline vs. the best-memory configuration; the x-axis begins at 40% to make differences visible. TGC alone understates the larger SGC gains — see the SGC columns in the table below.

The figure plots TGC to keep it readable; the table adds the stricter SGC metric, where the gains are often larger:.

Recent findings suggest that reading the SGC column, the stricter metric usually moves more than TGC — DeepSeek's SGC jumps +16.1pp against a +9.5pp TGC gain — because good guidelines especially help an agent clear every variant of a scenario, not just the average case. And the effect doesn't disappear at the top of the range: GPT-5.5 and Opus, both near the ceiling on TGC, still gain +7.2 and +7.1pp SGC respectively. Memory keeps paying off as long as a model has a remaining failure mode to target.

Recent findings suggest that A practical concern: injecting a full guideline set inflates every ReAct step's input, because the guidelines are re-sent each turn. Here's what we observed:.

Table 1. Average token use per task, accumulated across agent steps, measured against the no-memory baseline.

Curated retrieval keeps cost near baseline. For weaker models, where selection wins on accuracy, it also wins on cost — the best of both worlds (+16.1pp TGC at only +5% tokens for gpt-oss-120b). Better performance here does not require more inference cost.

According to recent reports, memory doesn't blow up the reasoning loop. DeepSeek runs about the same number of ReAct steps with memory as without (≈18–19 on average), so the added cost is input-token inflation, not longer trajectories.

The real efficiency lever in production is prompt caching: the static portion of the guideline set is identical across steps and can be cached, cutting effective cost substantially. Cache-aware prompt design — keeping the shared guideline-set prefix stable so it stays cacheable — is worth engineering for. We also hypothesize that context-window size plays a role: models with larger windows may absorb the full guideline set more effectively, while smaller-context models benefit more from retrieval that keeps injected content compact. We have not yet run controlled experiments isolating this factor.

It has been revealed that the lesson isn't to give an agent everything it has learned. It's to give it the amount of experience it can actually use.

For weak models, that means a compact core plus a few task-specific lessons — which, conveniently, is also the cheapest option.

For strong models with headroom, it means preserving the full guideline set, kept affordable in production via prompt caching.

For saturated models, it means spending no extra context until their remaining failure modes are better understood.

The gains are real across the board — automatic, leakage-free, and requiring no human annotation — but only when the dose fits the model.

This is a starting point, not the finish line:.

A learned selector. Our current retrieval ranks guidelines by cosine similarity, which we've shown doesn't perfectly predict which guidelines help a given task. A selector trained on outcome signal is the natural next step.

Industry observers note that memory for very weak models. Below a minimum capability baseline, self-distillation lacks signal. Teacher-distilled memory for very weak models is a separate problem we're exploring.

Sources indicate that beyond AppWorld. These results are validated on AppWorld — a rigorous multi-step benchmark, but a single one. Broader agent benchmarks and real-world deployments are in progress.

Isolating context window. As above, we want controlled experiments that separate context-window size from raw capability.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld tasks are graded by two metrics, both reported as percentages (higher is better):.

It has been revealed that TGC — Task Goal Completion. The share of individual tasks the agent completes fully and correctly. This is the headline "did it get the job done" number.

SGC — Scenario Goal Completion. A stricter, all-or-nothing metric. Each scenario bundles several variants of the same task (the same request with different data, phrasing, or edge conditions). SGC counts a scenario as passing only if the agent succeeds on every variant. It measures reliability — an agent that solves a task most of the time but fails on one variant scores on TGC but not on SGC.

Really interesting take on agentic memory. The idea that memory needs to be calibrated to the model rather than simply accumulated is especially useful for production systems. Selective retrieval also seems like a practical way to improve reliability without unnecessarily increasing context and inference costs. It makes a strong case for thoughtful custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions, where memory, performance, and cost all need to be designed together. https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-organization.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

GKE Dataplane V2 is Google Cloud’s next-generation networking dataplane for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium to replace traditional iptables routing and kube-proxy. We built GKE Dataplane V2 to meet the performance, scalability, and security demands of modern cloud-native workloads.

GKE customers consistently tell us that while they want to adopt GKE Dataplane V2 for its performance and scale, migrating production clusters carrying stateful workloads and established IP allocations has been challenging, often requiring a disruptive parallel cluster setup. Today, we are pleased to introduce the preview of in-place migration, allowing you to transition eligible VPC-native clusters from GKE Dataplane V1 to GKE Dataplane V2 directly.

Let’s take a look at what GKE Dataplane V2 brings to the table and how to start migrating your environment to it.

According to recent reports, GKE Dataplane V2 is built on the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium, with features specifically tuned for performance, scalability, and deep integration with Google Cloud networking. Consider the following capabilities:.

In a recent development, scale and performance: By handling packet processing with eBPF maps in the Linux kernel instead of linear iptables rules, GKE Dataplane V2 supports clusters of up to 15,000 nodes with network policy enforcement (and up to 65,000 nodes when network policy enforcement is disabled, which requires recreating clusters). This architecture also handles the high Pod churn, fast sandbox provisioning, and network identity scaling required by large agentic AI workloads.

High-throughput accelerator networking: Serves as the foundational networking layer for GPU and Cloud TPU clusters on GKE, helping keep accelerators computing rather than waiting on network initialization. It also powers capabilities like GKE managed DRANET for Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) of network devices.

It has been revealed that network security and observability: With GKE Dataplane V2, standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement and hierarchical ClusterNetworkPolicy work directly in the kernel with optimized performance. GKE Dataplane V2 also provides the underlying dataplane for sidecarless GKE ambient networking, while GKE Dataplane V2 observability delivers native network policy logging, live traffic topology, and Hubble flow metrics.

Instead of having to manually move workloads to a latest cluster, GKE now automates the transition across three stages, as described in the GKE Dataplane V2 migration guide:.

1. Eligibility and preflight checks: Before starting, verify that your Pod IP ranges have enough capacity to recreate the nodes by using GKE IP address utilization insights, and check Active Assist for incompatible configurations like custom eBPF programs on managed interfaces.

2. Initiate the migration: Once you’ve verified the preflight checks, start the migration with a single Google Cloud CLI patch command.

To initiate the migration on an eligible cluster, run:.

3. Automated rollout and finalization: GKE updates your node pools to GKE Dataplane V2 while respecting your configured maintenance windows, exclusions, and upgrade strategies. To move faster, you can also patch specific node pools manually, or roll back to GKE Dataplane V1 at any time prior to finalization.

In-place migration supports VPC-native clusters running GKE 1.35 or later (see the migration guide for exact version requirements). It does not support routes-based clusters or clusters running Calico.

In a recent development, in-place migration to GKE Dataplane V2 is available now in preview. During this time, we recommend testing migrations on non-production or test clusters first as you proposal your broader transition.

To learn more about GKE Dataplane V2 and to get started:.

Review cluster eligibility and migration phases in About migrating to GKE Dataplane V2.

Follow the instructions in Migrate VPC-native clusters to GKE Dataplane V2.

arXiv:2611.32663v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Can artificial intelligence reproduce the economic dynamics that emerge as households, firms and governments interact and adapt through markets and institutions? To answer this question, we define an economic world model (EWM) as an agent's internal representation of how an economic system works, enabling counterfactual simulation and decision-making under resource constraints. We then propose a general framework for studying EWMs that links three tasks: simulating agent behaviour, learning economic transitions and systematically evaluating the dynamics. As an initial implementation, we learn household policies from microeconomic data and calibrate a structural economic transition model using macroeconomic data, linking individual decisions to aggregate dynamics. Our micro-to-macro evaluation framework compares simulated individual actions and group distributions with observed microdata and assesses macroeconomic dynamics through forecasting and counterfactual experiments. Results show that simulated and observed household consumption distributions overlap by 94.9%, while EWM forecasts closely track real GDP and several other aggregate levels. In government-borrowing counterfactuals, the EWM reproduces the benchmark life-cycle model's short-run transmission from borrowing to consumption. For ex ante planning, the EWM enables an LLM agent to achieve 10.29% higher simulated GDP under the epidemic shock than direct LLM decisions. This initial EWM is only a starting point. We invite economists and AI researchers to build a stronger EWM together. Economists can contribute richer economic models and knowledge, while AI researchers can develop stronger data-driven methods for simulating agent behaviour and learning economic transitions. Together, we aim not only to reproduce real economic dynamics, but also to discover and test new mechanisms that support better decisions and benefit society.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:.

The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:.

Recent findings suggest that we follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

According to recent reports, we measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

For LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

Running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:.

Then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

Recent findings suggest that the block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:.

We can’t wait to see what you build.

arXiv:2611.32657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces. To make resection geometry learnable and editable, GeoSurge maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar. Using this grammar, anatomy-oriented and tumor-centered templates generate candidates, which are filtered by hard constraints and semantic deduplication. Training supervision is then derived from candidate-expert geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics. At inference, the reasoner uses patient evidence and surgical requirements to select or revise an action, which an independent geometry engine subsequently materializes and verifies. GeoSurge achieves the best overall scores on DeepTumour Liver and CRLM-QA, improving the constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench.

  • However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

In a recent development, one reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

It has been revealed that our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

Sources indicate that in some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

Sources indicate that for example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a newly introduced parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

According to recent reports, the reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually claims the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Voice clone of the same speaker.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff.

According to recent reports, parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

Industry observers note that to build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Sources indicate that some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:.

2011 draft budget (masked numbers).

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Recent findings suggest that our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11.

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11.

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Recent findings suggest that our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister.".

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

Sources indicate that for people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Recent findings suggest that public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to fresh audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.32646v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Official statistics are critical datasets for a wide variety of actors, including policymakers and businesses. For providers of official statistics, improving accessibility, governance, and disclosure of their data is of key importance. This can be improved by providing question-answering systems based on text-to-SQL approaches. However, existing text-to-SQL benchmarks do not resemble this setting. Official statistics are published as open-domain catalogs of thousands of wide tables whose columns and values are codes, and whose meaning is recorded in separate metadata rather than in a relational schema. To address this gap, we introduce LOCuST, a text-to-SQL benchmark that pairs over two thousand English and Dutch tables from Statistics Netherlands with a semantic knowledge graph. The graph describes the tables, measures, and dimension codes through labels, definitions, hierarchies, and units, and is the external knowledge a system needs to find the right tables and ground a question in the right codes. The benchmark includes expert-annotated questions for different query and aggregation types, including raw value retrieval, summations, proportion calculations, and joins. Alongside standard evaluation measures, we introduce an observation F1 metric that measures how close a query is to the ground truth even when the answers are different. We evaluate a variety of state-of-the-art LLMs and find that they struggle to write SQL that answers the questions correctly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our newly introduced frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work.
  • GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a upcoming quality bar for AI in complex professional work.
  • On Agents’ Last Exam, which tests multistep professional work, GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT‑6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our newly introduced frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. Both models deliver better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done within your usage limits. For businesses and developers, that means frontier performance at costs that make sense at scale.

GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a upcoming quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.

On Agents’ Last Exam, which tests multistep professional work, GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT‑6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.

It has been revealed that agents’ Last Exam evaluates models on long-horizon professional workflows. Its leaderboard results for Fable 5.2 exclude nine tasks that used a fallback model.

We believe GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. It sets a new high on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which tests how well models can carry out scientific work in a terminal. GPT-6.2 Astra scores 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than one-third the cost. It also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which asks models to interpret real biological data and run experiments to infer how a simulated system works.

Recent findings suggest that in the API, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT‑6 Astra’s, with a 60% discount on cached input ($8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens). GPT‑6.2 Sol keeps GPT‑6.1 Sol’s API token prices. On several benchmarks, both models come close to or outperform other leading models at a small fraction of the cost per task.

Compared with GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6.2 Sol is smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid strategy. It powers through multistep agentic workflows, writes clearly and naturally, and is intuitive to collaborate with. Many employees at OpenAI use it as their default model for both technical and non-technical tasks.

In Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0, GPT‑6.2 Sol comes within 0.5 points of GPT‑6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost (both at max).

FrontierCode 2.0 evaluates whether changes to real codebases meet maintainers’ standards for merging.

Its speed and intelligence also make it ideal for the important tasks people turn to AI for outside of work. On our recently released LifeVal⁠ evaluation, which measures performance on challenging everyday tasks, GPT‑6.2 Sol outscores GPT‑6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost.

LifeVal tests how well models handle everyday tasks tailored to someone’s needs, such as shortlisting kindergartens after a move, finding a home that fits a family’s budget and commute, or planning meals for a parent adjusting to a newly introduced diagnosis.

We trained GPT‑6.2 Astra to create clearer, better-designed slides, spreadsheets, and documents that more closely follow the conventions professionals use in fields like law, sales, finance, and accounting. The writing is more direct and specific, with fewer generic takeaways and less filler.

It has been revealed that harvey LAB‑AA v1.1 uses legal assignments to test whether models can find the relevant facts across source documents, apply them to a detailed brief, and produce an accurate deliverable that meets every requirement. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a upcoming state of the art, more than doubling Claude Fable 5.2’s pass rate at about one-sixth the cost. Astra for Law⁠, our configuration of GPT-6.2 Astra for lawyers, scores even higher on this benchmark.

According to recent reports, harvey LAB‑AA tests legal work such as reviewing contract provisions. Its headline score gives credit only when a deliverable meets every grading criterion and contains no material hallucinations.

Our internal GDPval v2 benchmark is our next iteration of GDPval⁠ that measures complex, long-horizon workflows from real projects in sectors like consulting, finance, and design. GPT‑6.2 Astra leads the models we tested, up 6.2 percentage points from GPT‑6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens. GPT‑6.2 Sol improves 5.3 points from GPT‑6.1 Sol.

GDPval v2 consists of long-horizon knowledge-work assignments from real projects in sectors like finance, data science, biotechnology, and marketing.

Building a valuation workbook or writing an investment memo starts with finding the relevant figures in source files and working out how they fit together. Artificial Analysis’s AA‑AnalystAgent tests that work on real spreadsheets and reports. In one task, models use California Medicaid’s expenditure reports to calculate how much the program spent on medical transport. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a fresh high, answering 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts.

GPT‑6.2 Astra is our best model yet at designing slides and following slide templates, whether given an original file or even a screenshot. It can match the layout, colors, and typography down to the exact font size, and carry the template’s writing style into latest slides. Early testers found the decks easier to use directly with fewer edits, thanks to titles that state the main takeaway and concise body copy that focuses on the details readers need.

Recent findings suggest that we evaluated GPT-6.2 Astra on turning dense information into readable briefs and infographics for both technical and non-technical audiences. Examples included trading briefs and diagrams of agentic workflows.

GPT-6.2 Astra's documents were a significant step up from GPT-6 Astra. The writing and charts made it much easier to pick out the key points of a briefing, and the diagrams clarified complex systems by showing how the parts work together.

In our Agent evals, GPT-6.2 Astra used 62% fewer tokens than GPT-6.1 Sol on complex legal-agent tasks. Astra was strongest on legal research, scoring higher than alternative models on 8 of the 10 research tasks we tested, across tax, M&A and litigation work.

GPT-6.2 Astra is a notable step up from GPT-6 Astra, completing more than 3x as many Legal Agent Benchmark tasks in our evaluations with 34.5% fewer output tokens. For internal memos drafting tasks, GPT-6.2 Astra caught more weaknesses in the client’s position, and drafted filings made fewer unwarranted concessions.

On the apps, dashboards and slides ClickUp Brain builds inside the workspace, GPT-6.2 Astra edged out our production model in blind testing. What stood out was how it got there: about 40% fewer tokens and 30% fewer review rounds.

GPT‑6.2 Astra’s more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. Engineers can use that additional detail to check how components fit, see where loads shift as a design moves, and test revisions before building a prototype.

Sources indicate that we asked GPT‑6.2 Astra to visualize chassis dynamics of a car on a mountain road. Astra created the 3D model and wrote a Python solver to simulate complex dynamics between the tires and suspension, then animated the results in Blender. This enables engineers to swiftly test fresh designs and improve simulation accuracy over time.

GPT‑6.2 Astra can model a mechanical system part by part, giving engineers a way to show how it goes together and test how design changes affect its behavior.

Recent findings suggest that our team used GPT‑6.2 Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago’s Marina City towers into a lamp. The video follows the design from reference photos through CAD revisions to a physical lamp assembled by hand. The site, generated by GPT-6.2 Astra, can be used to create your own paper lamp.

GPT‑6.2 Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look and building elements around the actual goal of the site.

According to recent reports, those gains in visual reasoning and computer use carry over to 3D design. GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol can turn a written brief into an interactive browser experience, from a pinball table you can play to a recreation of the Colosseum you can explore from different angles. On Artificial Analysis’s AA‑3D, human judges try two blinded experiences built from the same prompt and vote for the one they prefer. GPT‑6.2 Astra ranks first with 1,318 Elo, followed by Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271 and GPT‑6.2 Sol at 1,259.

Sources indicate that GPT-6.2 Astra is a huge leap forward for creative work. It makes Higgsfield Miracle possible, powering real-time video editing with pixel-level precision and giving creators ultimate creative control. In our internal 3D generation evals, it achieved the target result in one shot in 73% of cases, while GPT-6 Astra needed three or more iterations. This saves our creative team a lot of time and allows for more efficient fully agentic workflows.

GPT‑6.2 Astra has better judgment about how to execute a task, including matching its tools and effort to the workflow, and knowing when to use plugins versus computer use.

On coding, GPT-6.2 Astra is better at implementing and testing complex changes in existing codebases. Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision.

Recent findings suggest that GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol mark another significant jump in cyber capabilities. They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations. Like GPT‑6 Astra⁠, 6.2 Astra and Sol meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework⁠.

Due to their increased capabilities, we’re launching GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance. These protections reduce misuse risk, but also restrict some legitimate vulnerability research and security testing workflows. Through OpenAI Daybreak⁠, defenders can right now access GPT‑6 Sol with reduced cyber refusals on Daybreak Blue, in addition to our alpha for GPT-6 Astra, and GPT‑6 Cyber⁠ for advanced, authorized security testing on Daybreak Red. We will work to bring GPT‑6.2 models to Daybreak.

Recent findings suggest that we highlight key benchmark results below, using internal testing configurations with cybersecurity safeguards and classifiers disabled. See the accompanying system card⁠(opens in a fresh window) for full results and methodology.

Recent findings suggest that developers increasingly rely on coding agents to write production software, even as more capable agents lower the barrier to finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. PHP2Shell⁠(opens in a upcoming window) highlighted how AI can help researchers uncover critical flaws. With GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol, we made defensive capabilities a core focus, introducing new training signals to help developers prevent and repair those flaws—writing secure code from the start and producing patches that preserve intended behavior.

We're deploying GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with our strongest safeguards to date. We've tightened restrictions and strengthened the systems we use to monitor models⁠ and intervene when needed⁠.

Recent findings suggest that like GPT-6 Astra, in addition to meeting the Critical threshold for cybersecurity, both GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meet the High threshold for biological and chemical capabilities under our Preparedness Framework⁠. We’ve implemented protections to mitigate the associated risks, alongside increased restrictions across a set of potential dual-use biological and cybersecurity requests.

More details about our safeguards and testing are available in the GPT-6.2 system card⁠(opens in a new window).

GPT-6.2 Astra is our first externally released model to meet the High threshold for AI Self-improvement, which measures a model’s ability to accelerate AI research. A ‘High’ designation reflects our assessment that the model’s impact is equivalent to giving every OpenAI researcher an additional, highly capable research engineer as an assistant, relative to their 2024 baseline. We track this capability because models that can help develop future AI systems could also introduce new risks to safety, like accelerating progress faster than safeguards or human oversight can adapt.

In a recent development, to address these risks, we’ve built more oversight and controls into how we train and deploy our models. Before expanding internal access to GPT-6.2 Astra, we evaluated its alignment and verified that required safeguards were in place at each stage. We strengthened containment in our research environments⁠, and tested those protections with our most capable models. We also built Control Room⁠, a system that tracks research workloads and can halt further model output when intervention is needed. Our expanded monitoring⁠ examines models’ reasoning and actions across internal workloads and supported external deployments. It can automatically flag unauthorized behavior, and, where supported, pause workloads or conversations.

Both models performed similarly to GPT-6 Astra on most alignment evaluations, and took fewer improper actions in simulated workplace tasks. However, in two tests, they were more likely to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work, such as a missing file or unavailable search tool. We added instructions in Codex that substantially reduce these omissions, and we’re continuing to investigate the behavior.

In a recent development, GPT‑6.2 Astra costs significantly less per task than GPT‑6 Astra, driven by better token efficiency, a 20% discount on input and output tokens, and a deeper 60% discount on cached input tokens. Standard API rates per million tokens are $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output. GPT‑6.2 Sol carries forward GPT‑6.1 Sol’s rates of $2 for input, $0.10 for cached input, and $10 for output per million tokens.

For GPT-6.2 Astra & Sol, in order to improve cache reuse, help lower costs and latency, and preserve reasoning across turns, we recommend keeping prompt prefixes unchanged and appending upcoming instructions⁠(opens in a new window) to the conversation.

Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 results for Fable 5.2 are as reported by Artificial Analysis⁠(opens in a latest window) in the mini-swe-agent harness. Anthropic reported Fable 5.2's score of 74.6% at max reasoning in Claude Code.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.32508v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are advancing the automation of data-driven scientific research. Recent advances in recursive self-improvement (RSI) offer the potential for these agents to continuously improve through experience, but evaluating transfer across scientific tasks requires executable, scientifically verifiable tasks and independent assessment of self-improvement gains. We introduce RecurSciBench, a scalable benchmark for evaluating RSI in data-driven scientific research. Its RecurSciPipe framework automatically constructs scientific modeling and data analysis tasks from raw datasets, with execution-based verification and scientific validity checks. RecurSciBench spans four scientific domains, multiple data modalities, and varied scientific objectives. We evaluate four RSI systems by comparing their initial and evolved states on independent tasks after evolution on source tasks, covering within-type, cross-type, and cross-domain transfer. Experiments show that the benefits of self-improvement vary across agent systems and scientific domains. Positive overall gains can coexist with regressions on individual tasks. Experience can transfer across task types and benefit other domains even without measurable gains in the source domain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, 3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet).
  • Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can promptly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.
  • It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, 3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can promptly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond promptly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

In a recent development, for Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Sources indicate that papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:.

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:.

In a recent development, the expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:.

For each vector generation, we record:.

According to recent reports, our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:.

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Recent findings suggest that we sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:.

Sources indicate that each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

According to recent reports, for us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:.

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:.

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

This gives us several useful properties:.

In a recent development, only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

According to recent reports, we deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:.

It has been revealed that the HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:.

Sources indicate that if the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can rapidly see key analytics.

Industry observers note that for every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):.

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​.

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:.

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

In a recent development, launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:.

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Sources indicate that corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

Industry observers note that the revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Industry observers note that scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

According to recent reports, matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

Sources indicate that new generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

Recent findings suggest that the lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

arXiv:2611.32480v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Agent skills provide reusable workflows that guide LLM agents in using tools. Refining these workflows requires feedback on missing or incorrect instructions, but task-specific verifiers are not always available. We propose VISE (Verifier-Independent Skill Evolution), a scripts-first approach that uses tool implementations to guide skill revision. It extracts tool capabilities, input requirements, usage conditions, and output formats from source code. Using the task request and execution trace, it compares this information with current workflow instructions to identify missing or conflicting steps. It then recommends specific edits to SKILL.md, linking each change to the relevant implementation and usage conditions. We evaluate VISE as an additional revision stage for four evolution methods on SkillsBench and SkillLearnBench. Compared with the corresponding No-verifier conditions, it improves overall average task success by 9.14-13.35 percentage points. The proportion of tasks solved in all three runs increases by 12.36-18.29 points. A case study shows how revised instructions connect tool outputs to later steps. These results support tool implementations as a practical feedback source for skill self-evolution.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.32384v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop demonstrates how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.

Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

📅 25 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most interesting AI apps are pipelines.
  • gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface.
  • In a recent development, the best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something newly introduced. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

In a recent development, the best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Sources indicate that upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

👉 Try the Image Editor Pipeline.

One graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

It has been revealed that each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Sources indicate that every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

According to recent reports, decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

It has been revealed that check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

It has been revealed that every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:.

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:.

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:.

It has been revealed that the fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:.

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

You can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇.

#36215. Advancing chip design with OpenAI models

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1156 w)
