Tech Report: Research acceleration: The jagged frontier

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves.
  • This report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI⁠, adding latest quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process.
  • We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report⁠, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves. Today, we’re providing an update on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI, based on internal measurements of how coding agents have accelerated and changed the AI development cycle.

This report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI⁠, adding latest quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process. Overall, we believe this patch provides a broader, though still partial, picture of how research at OpenAI is changing.

We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report⁠, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.

As capabilities improve and dramatic AI-driven research acceleration becomes increasingly possible, we will need to solve novel technical and governance issues to maintain human oversight and safely scale AI systems⁠. Transparency about indicators of RSI is therefore essential to inform a public discussion of the capabilities, risks, and required safeguards for increasingly powerful AI; however, our reporting should not be read as an intention to pursue full RSI. We have been heartened to see that several other organizations have recently contributed to the growing body of work measuring AI R&D acceleration1. Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance these shared measurement norms across the industry.

We structure this report in three sections, each focused on a different aspect of AI research:.

We believe organizing the results in this way provides a useful framework for reasoning about how AI is used in research and how that use might contribute to improvements in model capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that AI research uses several inputs, including data, AI tools (e.g., coding agents), human labor, and compute. In this report, we focus on AI tools as an input to research. Specifically, we document how the intensity of coding-agent use varies across teams and changes over time. Further, while we do not directly report changes in labor costs, we examine how the share of spending on research labor has changed relative to spending on other factors over time.

Since our first report⁠, agentic AI usage within the research organization has continued to increase exponentially. At API list prices, the median researcher now uses around $2,400 USD per day on agentic AI tools, and the 90th percentile researcher now around $23,000 USD per day, up 62% and 105% respectively from $1,500 and $11,000 in September.2 This trend in increased agentic usage captures a wide variety of changes including increased activity, shifts to more expensive models, and changes to model behavior and agentic harnesses.

Industry observers note that we next turn to the average number of “agent workdays” per researcher per day, where we define every eight hours of agent use as one agent workday. In contrast to agentic spend, agent workdays better capture the amount of “wall clock time” agents spend working, but do not account for changes in model capabilities or pricing.

Overall, agent workdays per researcher have risen from 0.5 agent workdays per researcher to 5.7 agent workdays per researcher, an elevenfold increase, with the largest increase in teams focused on pretraining and posttraining. On those teams, agent runtime averaged roughly eight workdays per researcher per calendar day. In scaling and infrastructure, the average was roughly four. We note that this workday metric generally includes interactive use only, so it may undercount automations.

Our September analysis⁠ highlighted increasing use of concurrent agents by researchers, including subagents and multiple sessions. We extend this analysis further in time and provide more granular bucketing. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of included researchers averaged a daily peak of at least four agents working concurrently and more than 10% averaged at least sixteen concurrent agents.

We next compare monthly API-equivalent spending on agentic AI use with monthly non-equity compensation for human researchers. We track this ratio to see how the allocation between agent and human labor changes as models become more capable. Although the ratio we report excludes equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers at OpenAI, we believe it still provides a partial yet informative view of this spending allocation.

Sources indicate that as of September 2026, the API-equivalent value of agentic AI use in OpenAI’s research organization was about twice its non-equity compensation, with higher ratios in pretraining and posttraining than in other parts of the research organization. Despite this, internal deployment, which combines internal Codex, ChatGPT, and API usage, accounts for only 2% of total research compute.

It has been revealed that labor costs include salary, overtime, bonuses, benefits, and employer taxes. Equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers, is excluded.

Sources indicate that finally, we examine how researchers allocate their time across research areas. We first collected individual-level contributions from researchers in the form of organization-public Slack posts, pull requests, and internal documents from January through September 2026. We then used classifiers to group these contributions into research areas, and each researcher-week was divided equally across that researcher’s verified projects for the week. This provides a proxy for where researchers were directing their attention.

Sources indicate that importantly, unlike our other analyses, the “research area” we classify here does not correspond to formal reporting lines. For example, a researcher on a posttraining team who spends half their time on infrastructure improvements would be estimated as contributing half a workweek to Scaling / Infrastructure Contributions and half to Posttraining Contributions. This allows us to create a robust measurement of where researchers are actively spending time even if they do not formally shift teams.

We find that the amount of researcher time dedicated to each of the areas we identify has grown over the course of 2026. Notably, using this methodology, we find that Safety & Alignment saw the largest absolute increase across any research area, almost doubling in documented workweek contributions since the start of the year due to a combination of fresh hires and existing researchers shifting their focus toward safety projects. This research area covers workstreams such as alignment evals, monitorability, and reward hacking research. A notable inflection point that we measure in the growth of Safety & Alignment coincides with the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, and OpenAI’s subsequent work to develop and improve safety cases for frontier AI training⁠.

Sources indicate that we note that the distinction between research areas, and especially posttraining versus safety and alignment, is nontrivial and we may iterate on the definition over time. The methods section below describes examples of high-level workstreams.

To better understand how agent use might affect research productivity, we next examine how the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI is changing. The productivity gains from fresh technologies depend in part on how work is reorganized around them. As agents improve, researchers may change which tasks they delegate to AI, how they oversee and coordinate agents’ work, and which projects they pursue. Below, we report both quantitative and qualitative measures of how AI is changing the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI. Together, these different types of data contribute to a (partial) view of how researchers are reorganizing their work around agents and how researchers remain in the loop today.

Our September analysis⁠ highlighted that agents became more likely to complete tasks successfully without human intervention, including tasks estimated to require several hours of human work. Using an updated methodology (see the methods section below), we find that this trend has generally continued. Importantly, as agents have become more capable, researchers may also have changed the types of tasks delegated within each duration bucket. As a result, changes in zero-intervention success rates within these buckets may reflect both capability improvements and researchers’ changing choices about when and how to use agents.

According to recent reports, alongside these trends by estimated duration, we also examine how success varies across the different types of tasks researchers might choose to delegate. We report estimated success rates by category and task, using the O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a new window) developed by Epoch AI. Unsurprisingly, our results suggest that models are not equally good across all task categories: for instance, from August 1, 2026 through October 18, 2026, estimated success rates without human intervention was higher for Communicate (69%) and Analyze (58%) than for Build (43%). Similarly at the task level, estimated success rates were higher for tasks such as monitoring runs for complications (79%) and answering technical questions (72%), whereas they were lower for writing code for inference and serving stacks (25%) and building evaluation, reinforcement-learning, and agent environments (29%). So long as model performance on AI R&D-related tasks is heterogeneous, lower-performing categories and tasks could become bottlenecks to high overall uplift.

Industry observers note that our September analysis⁠ reported how research employee AI use was split across output tokens using the same O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a new window). Below, we report how often researchers used coding agents for individual tasks. This puts relatively higher weight on short tasks such as answering technical questions compared to token-intensive tasks such as launching and monitoring a training run or implementing a complex feature.

Industry observers note that we next turn to researchers’ own assessments of how AI is changing their work. Through surveys and interviews, we examine how researchers value coding agents, how they come up with research ideas, and how they have adapted their workflows.

From late August to early September 2026, we conducted a survey of 101 research staff to understand AI uplift, centered around the following hypothetical: “Suppose your team’s access to all coding agents better than GPT-5.2 was revoked for the next 3 months. How much would you trade to restore frontier coding agents?” The median researcher reported being willing to trade:.

In a recent development, researchers also reported that their team would need a median of three months to complete work of equal value to their last month of work if they were not allowed to use coding agents (i.e., if they were only allowed to use GitHub Copilot + ChatGPT). While it is key to note potential challenges with the accuracy of self-reports, as well as the ad-hoc nature of our survey sampling strategy, these results are consistent with researchers attributing significant value to AI uplift in their work.

Bars show the weighted share of answers in each range. Dashed lines mark the weighted medians.

In a separate survey in late October, we also asked whether respondents expected to be more productive in their daily work with our latest internal model or with help from both a mid-career human research engineer and a 2024 model such as o1-preview. 27 of the 28 respondents chose or leaned toward the latest internal model. The remaining respondent did not choose between the two options as posed and said they would pick GPT-6 Astra over the human-assisted option.

In a recent development, we are also interested in tracking progress in AI-driven idea generation, since the ability to develop and vet conceptual research ideas (research taste) may be a bottleneck for recursive self-improvement. To measure this, we asked one to four researchers who made key contributions in each of three areas (pretraining, posttraining, and safety monitoring) to name one to three ideas they considered most key to the GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra releases. We then asked how those ideas originated and what role, if any, AI played in developing them.

In a recent development, for both releases, posttraining and safety monitoring researchers said that, to their knowledge, people came up with all the ideas they named, and models helped implement them. Pretraining researchers likewise attributed the ideas they identified for GPT-6 Astra entirely to people.

For GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers described developing ideas in conversation with Codex. One credited Codex with identifying key insights as they worked through an idea together. Another mentioned the main idea was theirs, but it only started working well after Codex suggested a change.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, to capture qualitative evidence on workflow changes, we also interviewed ten researchers from pretraining, posttraining, and safety on how they used agents. Across these interviews, five main themes emerged, which we summarize below:.

Recent findings suggest that beyond changes in research inputs and workflows, we also want to understand whether AI use is accelerating research progress. To inform this question, we present three measures. Two of them—lines of code and the number of research experiments—were included in our September analysis⁠. These measures are straightforward to track, but increases in these measures of research activity do not necessarily imply faster research progress. We therefore also introduce OpenAI ECI, an OpenAI-specific internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, which is one methodology to track changes in model capabilities as a more direct measure of research outcomes.

Industry observers note that we first report how many lines of code are changed per active contributor over time. This measure has continued to increase sharply during 2026 relative to the pre-2025 average. Note that we have made several methodological updates since our September analysis⁠. We now show a 28-day trailing average instead of quarterly averages, providing a more detailed view of changes over time. We have also revised the criteria for which code changes we include (in particular excluding tests), as described in Methods .

Industry observers note that as in our September report⁠, we also track the number of experiments run per active experimenter over time. Over the four weeks ending October 18, logged experiments per active experimenter averaged 1.68 times the 2025 baseline.

Lastly, we report progress on a metric meant to capture advancements in the capabilities of our models. The Epoch Capabilities Index⁠(opens in a new window) is widely used to measure the progress trend in general AI capabilities. The methodology behind OpenAI ECI (OECI) is very similar to Epoch’s methodology, but OECI uses a combination of public benchmarks and OpenAI internal benchmarks. Here, we graph the OECI of 20 publicly released OpenAI models and 28 other models.

According to recent reports, we find that the OECI frontier for OpenAI models has increased by 16.4 points per year since August 2025, compared to a trend that Epoch observed of 14 points per year⁠(opens in a fresh window) since late 2024. Note that OpenAI models score higher relative to competitors on OECI than they do on Epoch’s ECI, likely due to differences in the benchmark mixture.

We plan to continue monitoring OpenAI ECI and other top-level capability metrics to determine whether capabilities progress is accelerating due to RSI.

Vertical lines are 90% bootstrap intervals. The trendline is fit on the 9 record-setting OpenAI releases.

Overall, our findings extend the picture from our September report⁠: researchers are using agents more intensively, delegating more work, and adapting their workflows around models’ capabilities and limitations. However, this uplift isn’t uniform across all research workflows, and agents today still have significant flaws.

Industry observers note that we note that the historical trends and metrics we report (which involve significant human-AI collaboration) may not be predictive of future AI-driven progress. For instance, we recently saw sudden and rapid breakthroughs in mathematics⁠ produced by frontier models. As our models become increasingly autonomous and capable for research, we are monitoring for similarly rapid breakthroughs in deep learning.

In a recent development, importantly, as AI becomes better at improving itself, competitive pressures and governance challenges will increase, and a key task⁠ will be to ensure humanity remains a part of the process. We hope releasing this data will inform discussions on pacing model capabilities and the governance of recursive self-improvement.

Industry observers note that going forward, we will continue to refine the methods underlying the metrics reported here. We also hope to expand our reporting to provide additional information in a number of areas, including, but not limited to:.

While the science of empirically measuring AI R&D acceleration is relatively young, it is rapidly growing across the research frontier. So far, Anthropic has independently released three⁠(opens in a new window) separate⁠(opens in a new window) reports⁠(opens in a new window) documenting how internal model deployments have accelerated the AI research process. Section 3.4.2 of the Gemini 4 Argon Safety and Security Report⁠(opens in a new window) outlines empirically the growing share of AI-written code internally at Google DeepMind. In collaboration with Anthropic, METR released an acceleration report⁠(opens in a new window) estimating the amount that internal Claude models have accelerated the capabilities frontier.

We note that OpenAI researchers do not right now have agentic coding quotas.

It has been revealed that on August 21st, OpenAI internally deployed a temporary harness efficiency improvement. We found that this internal deployment coincided with a sharp decrease in input token utilization, which appears to have severely depressed the documented amount of internal token spend. This harness change was gradually reverted across internal deployments for reasons unrelated to spend starting on September 10th, and we find that token spend rapidly increases afterwards.

Industry News: More Powerful, Less Verifiable? Mitigating Hard-to-Verify Hallucinations in MLLM's Reinforcement Learning

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (180 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.32055v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) strengthens model capabilities through feedback from humans and environments. However, emerging evidence suggests that reward optimization can produce outputs whose errors are harder for humans to detect. To address this issue, we construct ITHV (the Image-Text Hallucination Verifiability Dataset), comprising 2,728 visually grounded instances that distinguish between obvious hallucinations, which humans readily detect, and elusive hallucinations, which humans struggle to identify. We then propose DAPO-V, an extension of DAPO that maximizes correctness subject to a budget on verifiability-aware risk. Specifically, DAPO-V combines a verifiability-aware reward with adaptive dual control, where larger penalties are assigned to incorrect responses on questions with lower human verification accuracy. An adaptive multiplier further adjusts the penalty strength according to risk-budget violations. Across three MLLM base models, DAPO-V improves overall accuracy while substantially improving accuracy on elusive hallucination questions by 5.78--9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO. We further test DAPO-V with a blinded human study, which shows that hallucinations are more readily detected in DAPO-V than those of the base model.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that amazon S3 Vectors now supports up to 40 KB of filterable metadata per vector, up from 2 KB.
  • According to recent reports, S3 Vectors provides native support to store and query vectors in Amazon S3, delivering purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage and query at billion-vector scale.
  • In a recent development, the higher filterable metadata limit is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available.

It has been revealed that amazon S3 Vectors now supports up to 40 KB of filterable metadata per vector, up from 2 KB. You can attach and filter on more attributes per vector, such as category, permissions, timestamps, and descriptive tags, so your retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic, and semantic-search applications can narrow results by more of the fields that matter to them.

According to recent reports, S3 Vectors provides native support to store and query vectors in Amazon S3, delivering purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage and query at billion-vector scale. With this launch, indexes in upcoming vector buckets support the higher limit by default, with no change to how you write vectors with PutVectors or run filtered queries with QueryVectors. To use the higher limit on an existing index, upgrade it in place to enhanced index mode with the UpdateIndexMode API.

In a recent development, the higher filterable metadata limit is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available. To get started, use the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the Amazon S3 console. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation.

Tech Report: Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • Sources indicate that earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • It has been revealed that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

It has been revealed that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

Recent findings suggest that that is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with upcoming runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

Recent findings suggest that from there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the upcoming one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and highlights exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:.

Sources indicate that the agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Industry observers note that before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

It has been revealed that funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent indicates so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Recent findings suggest that claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

According to recent reports, published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

According to recent reports, A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

In a recent development, funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

Recent findings suggest that funes is open source too. Open an glitch for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Sources indicate that ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

It has been revealed that full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

EffectWAM: Learning Action-Grounded Effects for Robot Manipulation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.32053v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: World-action models connect visual prediction with executable robot control. We present EffectWAM, which develops this connection through three complementary components: Effect, camera positional encoding (CaPE), and Action Grounding. Effect represents visual change as the difference between independently encoded future observations and a shared current-observation anchor. CaPE conditions endpoint pooling on relative camera pose when reliable extrinsics are available, while sharing the same learned parameters with pose-free pooling for uncalibrated trajectories. Action Grounding trains the visual representation to retain measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state. An exponential moving average of the observation encoder supplies Effect targets. A shared generation expert learns to jointly predict Effect and an executable action chunk through flow matching, and reuses the sampled pair to generate future video on demand. This allows the controller to execute actions without waiting for video synthesis. We train on more than 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, excluding unused chain-of-thought data, and accommodate dataset-specific joint, end-effector, and hand-pose representations. Our evaluation uses the Small (8B) configuration on all five benchmarks and additionally evaluates the Large (26B) configuration on RoboDojo. Experiments examine closed-loop manipulation across complementary benchmarks, and comparisons across multiple baseline policies show consistent improvements from Action Grounding.

  • Industry observers note that email alerts can go unnoticed when builders are away from their inbox, leaving little time to respond before a project is paused.
  • Recent findings suggest that to turn on SMS alerts, verify your mobile phone number in AWS Settings and turn on text alerts for spend limits.

Industry observers note that builders using the newly introduced AWS experience on the Paid initiative can now receive spend limit alerts by text message (SMS), alongside existing email notifications. A spend limit sets the maximum monthly cost for a project. Notifications are sent as a project approaches its limit, and when a project reaches its limit, AWS automatically pauses it. SMS gives builders a second way to stay informed about their project costs.

Industry observers note that email alerts can go unnoticed when builders are away from their inbox, leaving little time to respond before a project is paused. SMS alerts close this gap with a text message when a project's actual costs reach 90% of its spend limit, so builders have time to act, such as raising the limit or stopping resources they don't need.

Recent findings suggest that to turn on SMS alerts, verify your mobile phone number in AWS Settings and turn on text alerts for spend limits. Text alerts are only sent to verified numbers, and you can opt out at any time. SMS alerts for spend limits are available at no additional charge for US phone numbers, including Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands, and American Samoa.

To learn more, see Create a spend limit in AWS Settings, the AWS Account Management Reference Guide, or Get started with AWS.

While heterogeneous multi-modal meteorological early warnings often contain decision-critical information for UDS RTC, none of the existing approaches can exploit such externally-sourced information within the control workflow. Here we introduce AgenticAI-Control, an agentic artificial intelligence framework able to assimilate multi-source meteorological early warnings in RTC. Two coupled large language model agents are integrated to generate control strategies by retrieving meteorological early-warnings and fusing them with domain engineering expertise. Validated via simulation studies of a combined sewer catchment in eastern China across 10 real-world rainfall events, the AgenticAI-Control achieved 69.1-90.6% reduction in aggregated flood and overflow volumes compared to the rule-based baseline control. Rigorously standardized prompt engineering and modular workflow constraints substantially compress performance disparities among four distinct LLMs. Our work establishes AgenticAI as a viable tool to unify multi-source meteorological monitoring and practitioner domain knowledge, surmounting longstanding monitoring limitations of UDS RTC and delivering cost-efficient, robust intelligent control solutions for sensor-sparse sewer infrastructures.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance.
  • Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own.
  • It has been revealed that note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

It has been revealed that note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:.

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:.

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:.

In a recent development, the IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

In a recent development, we use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:.

While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it indicates that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

Sources indicate that A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

arXiv:2611.32012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As frontier AI models and agents are deployed more broadly in the real world, marketing is emerging as one of their largest applications. Marketing teams use AI models to produce brand assets like website copy and social media posts, while consumers' agents autonomously discover products, research purchases, and navigate websites. However, evaluating marketing capability is difficult because unlike areas like software development, customer support, or legal review where ground truth is more objectively defined, marketing is subjective, and output quality is judged based on taste and brand. We introduce Marketing-Bench, the first open-source marketing benchmark, which pairs discriminative tasks (detecting brand anomalies) with generative tasks (remediation), while keeping answers verifiable. Marketing-Bench tests five key pillars: factuality, consistency, coherence, structure, and brand voice, all crucial elements for good brand content on the web. We find that frontier models are far from solving the benchmark: the average model corrects only about half of the introduced concerns (53.1%), whereas a marketing expert corrects nearly all of them. Even the strongest, GPT-6 Astra, reaches only 74.8%, with Claude Opus and Fable, Gemini Argon, and GPT-6 Sol falling well short. These findings suggest that marketing capabilities are less mature than adoption implies, and that principled evaluation should precede further scaling of usage. Marketing-Bench is a first step toward "frontier marketing models" with superhuman marketing performance.

If a inquiry needs a support engineer, the agents will gather details and create a case. This reduces the time partners spend looking for help, and gives support teams the context they need to resolve cases faster.

Partners can handle a case from start to finish in one chat, with the full record in AWS Support Center. To create a case, partners can start describing their matter to AWS Partner Central Agents or use the prompt "get support." The agents gather additional details necessary to resolve the case, set the category, and draft the description. Partners review and submit the case, and the agents route the case to the right support team. In the same chat, partners can view case communications, track progress, post replies, and add attachments. With this launch, Partner Central and AWS Marketplace cases also move to AWS Support Center. There, partners can view the full case history and translate support correspondence into Chinese, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced support experience is available today to all AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers in the AWS Partner Central console and through the AWS Partner Central Agents MCP server. With the MCP server, partners can bring the support experience into tools such as Kiro, AWS Quick, CRM systems, and other AI clients. #36164. TableRouter: Query-Aware Evidence Construction for Long-Table Question Answering

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (210 w)

TableRouter: Query-Aware Evidence Construction for Long-Table Question Answering

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (210 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.32006v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: LLMs can reason over tables, but when tables outgrow the context budget, retrieving relevant rows is only part of the solution. A retrieved subset may omit information required for an exact aggregate; even complete evidence may remain difficult for an LLM to use. We introduce TableRouter, a training-free framework that analyzes each query, then chooses between two routes: a computation route, which derives question-conditioned statistics from the full table, and a coverage route, which retrieves relevant rows and column summaries. The chosen context is passed to a frozen LLM in one call. Across three LLMs and three large-table benchmarks, TableRouter outperforms the strongest of six single-call baselines in all nine settings by 1.2-18.3 accuracy points, using 77-95% fewer estimated FLOPs than truncated-table prompting, with indexing amortized across questions. The gains extend to long tables from databases not used in earlier experiments, where TableRouter achieves 35.8% with Qwen2.5-7B, versus 16.4% for the strongest external baseline. A controlled experiment reveals that explicitly providing computed statistics improves accuracy by up to 40.0 points, even when all answer-determining rows are available. These results distinguish evidence access from evidence use: long-table reasoning depends on how information is represented, not only on which rows are retrieved.

Tech Report: NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • According to recent reports, neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

According to recent reports, neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

It has been revealed that neoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

In a recent development, neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

It has been revealed that we pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Sources indicate that pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

It has been revealed that to get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

It has been revealed that viDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

According to recent reports, late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

According to recent reports, we tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Owners can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding newly introduced documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

Industry observers note that so we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

In a recent development, neoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

Sources indicate that we provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers at the moment supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Industry observers note that visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

Industry observers note that neoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

The Blueprint: How Kult built a gaming companion that actually knows your game

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that welcome to The Blueprint, our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies.
  • Industry observers note that kult is a London-based startup building a companion experience for games.
  • According to recent reports, traditionally, getting help in the middle of a game meant alt-tabbing, opening a video, scrolling a forum, and hoping you find the answer before you forget why you looked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Recent findings suggest that welcome to The Blueprint, our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work.

Industry observers note that kult is a London-based startup building a companion experience for games. It sits alongside your session, understands the game you are playing and where you are in it, and answers by voice and on a second screen. The more you play with it, the better it knows how you like to play.

According to recent reports, traditionally, getting help in the middle of a game meant alt-tabbing, opening a video, scrolling a forum, and hoping you find the answer before you forget why you looked. Information should come to the player instead. As gamers ourselves, our team wanted a way for someone to be able to ask a question out loud, hands on the keyboard or controller, hear an answer, and consult a second screen if needed, without interrupting their immersion in the game.

Three things decide whether that works: latency, accuracy and cost.

Latency: Games are time-sensitive. The answer has to be fast, and the interaction should feel like asking a friend who’s an expert on the game, sitting on the couch next to you and watching you play.

Industry observers note that accuracy: General-purpose models have training cutoffs. They can be months out of date and are often wrong about a specific game, patch, or build — and a wrong answer can be costly in the game and a waste of the player's time. Every game also has its own items, systems, and vocabulary, so accuracy has to hold across hundreds of games. The right answer also depends on the player: The same question deserves a different answer 10 minutes into a game than a 100 hours in.

Cost: An always-on companion handles many turns per session, so every turn has to be inexpensive enough for a consumer product. Covering hundreds of games is only possible if adding one is cheap and takes no manual work.

Given these needs, we knew we would want a range of models to build Kult. Fortunately, Google’s Gemini models have some of the greatest variety in terms of balancing performance and especially cost, and with the Model Garden in Gemini platform, we have access to hundreds of models beyond Gemini. Gemini models have became the default family on both sides of the system: the live conversation, and the knowledge behind it, dynamically match the right model for every task.

The lightest Gemini Flash tier handles high-volume, repetitive work, where we make thousands of small calls for every game we add. Gemini Flash runs every conversational turn. It works out what the player is asking and writes an answer grounded in our knowledge of that game, fast enough to keep up with play. The latest and most advanced Gemini models handle the rare, heavy reasoning we do once per game.

It has been revealed that having that range on one API surface matters to a small team. The latest Gemini Flash models in particular sit at a point of price, speed, and quality that we have not found elsewhere, and they are the reason an always-on gaming companion works as a consumer product.

According to recent reports, we reach the models through both the Gemini platform and the Gemini Developer API, with a routing layer that picks the backend for each model. Our backend runs on Google Kubernetes Engine.

Every answer comes in two parts. The voice gives the short version. At the same moment, a visual answer lands in a feed on the player's second screen: images, embedded video, maps, builds, interactive tools made for that game, and links to the guides and creators behind the answer.

Sources indicate that we build that feed with Google's open standard for agent-generated interfaces. The model does not write code. It describes the interface it wants using a catalog of components we designed, and the app renders it natively in Kult's own style. That keeps the feed safe and consistent, and lets us add upcoming kinds of visual answers, and new devices, without rebuilding the front end.

Kult now covers more than 100 games, and adding a game is an automated process, not a manual project. That’s a key part of what lets a small team aim at any game a player picks up, including new releases, where most of the playing happens in the first weeks.

We are in alpha with our first players and opening up to more over the coming months. As we have grown, we have built a close working relationship with the Google Cloud team, with direct access to their engineers when we need it. That matters when every model generation raises the ceiling of what a gaming companion product can do.

This expertise, both within the models and our supportive partners, allows us to focus on our passion: building the features gamers want, faster and better than any possible competition.

Five principles shape how Kult works.

Answers come from knowledge we build, not from what a model happens to remember. A game can change with every patch. For each game we cover, Kult builds a structured knowledge base automatically and keeps it current, and the model's job is to reason over that knowledge.

Industry observers note that the answer depends on who is asking. Kult keeps track of your session: the game, what you have been doing, and what you asked a moment ago. "What is he weak to?" needs no further explanation, because Kult already knows which boss you’re facing. Over time it learns from how you play, what you ask about and what you ignore, and shapes its answers around you. A player who wants the fastest route and one who wants to find everything should not get the same replies.

The player is never left in silence. Kult responds straight away and carries the conversation while the deeper reasoning runs behind it. The spoken answer is short, and the visual feed carries everything the voice cannot.

The smallest model that can do the job does the job. Much of the work in a system like ours is a decision, not a piece of writing. It needs to understand which game the query is about, does the question need a lookup, did the answer cover the point.

In a recent development, for decisions like these we use Jev, a decision-only model that returns a choice with a calibrated confidence score. Confident cases are settled in a fraction of a second at a fraction of the cost, and uncertain ones escalate to a larger Gemini model. Every model sits behind a registry, so when a latest generation ships, we benchmark it against reference answers written by people who know the games, and swap it in if it wins.

Every question makes Kult better. Taken together, the questions players ask about a game show us where its knowledge is thin and what to build next. We are designing Kult so that this loop tightens with every session. The more people play, the richer the knowledge becomes for everyone. Every session teaches a player something, as well as the entire Kult system, and Kult helps them keep it. We think the companion that sits beside the game is only the start.

It has been revealed that next is computer vision. In the coming months, Kult will start to see what is happening in your game, so the companion can be aware of the moment without being asked. We’re using Google's Live models as part of that work, for video understanding and more.

If you are a gamer, try it for yourself www.joinkult.gg.

How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (263 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31990v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.

In a recent development, when Sumitomo Life’s planning teams prepare proposals for senior management, ChatGPT Enterprise helps them review source material and organize their findings. They combine those findings with firsthand information and draw on their expertise to decide what to recommend. Teams in accounting and finance also use ChatGPT for research and analysis.

The Japanese life insurer’s executives and managers were among the first to use ChatGPT. Their example and the president’s encouragement helped more employees try it in their own work.

Sumitomo Life began using generative AI at work in 2023. At first, employees mainly asked questions in chat. As they tested general-purpose AI tools, ChatGPT stood out for its range. They could use deep research to explore a question across sources and bring ChatGPT into work they were already doing in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel.

In a recent development, in 2025, about 100 to 150 people, including executives and members of planning teams, piloted ChatGPT Business. In June 2026, the tech giant moved to ChatGPT Enterprise. In planning a rollout to thousands of employees, the insurer weighed output quality, how well ChatGPT fit different kinds of work, and the security requirements of a financial institution.

It has been revealed that sumitomo Life worked with OpenAI to assess ChatGPT Enterprise against the insurer’s security standards. The review covered how Sumitomo Life could manage workspace access and feature permissions, along with OpenAI’s policy of excluding business data from model training by default. The insurer continues to decide how employees can use ChatGPT based on the information they handle and the systems they connect to.

Sumitomo Life’s investment teams use statistical analysis to forecast returns and assess risks such as price swings. ChatGPT helps analysts draft the code for that work, reducing the amount they need to write themselves.

Recent findings suggest that planning teams use ChatGPT to track developments at other Japanese insurers and find examples from overseas. They use that research to strengthen proposals for senior management.

According to recent reports, planning teams supplement public sources with firsthand information from people familiar with the work. They use projects in ChatGPT to keep the material together with related chats, files, and custom instructions.

Industry observers note that sumitomo Life’s president began using AI during the ChatGPT Business pilot. In management meetings and on the manufacturer’s internal portal, the president regularly encouraged employees to put it to work.

Sources indicate that kakeru Tateyama, a senior member of Sumitomo Life’s planning department, saw how that example shaped adoption. “When senior leaders don’t understand a latest technology, it can be hard to get it off the ground,” he claims. “Here, our executives and managers were among the first to use it. They saw for themselves what it could do. I think that made it easier for everyone else to start using it.”.

In a recent development, since the initial training, OpenAI has shared examples of how organizations around the world use ChatGPT. The teams discuss which approaches fit Sumitomo Life’s priorities and assess newly introduced features as they become available.

Sumitomo Life tracks how often employees use ChatGPT Enterprise and estimates the return on that investment.

Sources indicate that the insurer looks beyond the number of accounts it has issued. Its quarterly survey asks employees how often they use ChatGPT, which steps in their work they use it for, and whether they use it with colleagues.

In a recent development, estimated ROI based on employee-reported time savings. 524% applies only to employees using ChatGPT 101+ times per month; overall estimated ROI is 203%.

Sumitomo Life used employee-reported time savings to estimate ROI for different levels of ChatGPT use. The estimates were higher among more frequent customers. ROI averaged 55% for 8 to 15 uses per month, 231% for 16 to 30, and 524% for 101 or more. The overall average was 203%.

It has been revealed that employees are also beginning to take on work they previously lacked the time or specialist skills to tackle. For Sumitomo Life, that broadens what each person can contribute, even where the benefit is harder to capture in hours saved.

Sources indicate that masakazu Obi, a deputy general manager in the planning department, sees a larger opportunity in changing how the work itself gets done. “If we take our existing ways of working for granted, we won’t get the full benefit of AI,” he indicates. “The question is whether we can change the processes themselves. As we introduce AI, we’re also working to change those processes over the long term.”.

Sumitomo Life intends to start expanding AI use to more employees in the second half of fiscal 2026. For each role, it will identify which tasks AI can handle, where employees can work alongside it, and which responsibilities people should keep.

In a recent development, over the longer term, the insurer is considering AI for more specialized work, including underwriting and claims payments. It plans to explore latest technologies and services with OpenAI as it redesigns workflows with AI in mind.

The goal is to give employees more time to talk with customers. Sumitomo Life sees those conversations as part of its commitment to the well-being of both customers and employees.

Comparing models has usually meant reading model cards one at a time and relying on benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. You can also choose a use case profile and an optimization goal (balanced, cost, latency, or throughput) to see the metrics for the configuration you proposal to deploy. At launch, the leaderboard covers more than 70 LLMs from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee.

Recent findings suggest that the JumpStart model leaderboard is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is available. It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shared last-level caches (LLCs) increasingly dominate server processor die area, forcing architects to trade core counts for cache capacity. While intelligent data prefetching offers a pathway to reclaim this silicon, designing coordinated, multi-level prefetching policies for multi-core systems is bottlenecked by day-long, cycle-level simulations. This simulation wall limits even LLM-based microarchitecture discovery; the state-of-the-art ArchAgent system evolves one cache level at a time on single-core benchmarks, adds multi-core configurations only at the end, and trails the human champion under multi-core shared cache contention. We introduce DuoArchitect, an autonomous agentic framework for multi-fidelity, multi-core co-discovery of prefetchers. Agents jointly evolve evaluation proxies and coordinated prefetching policies across the L1D, L2, and LLC hierarchies, constructing simulation proxies 3-26x faster than cluster evaluation and hardware diagnostic oracles to guide the search. To study how much cache silicon a smarter prefetcher can replace, we evaluate and evolve prefetchers under reduced cache budgets, and find that evolving under our tightest cache constraint (with both the L2 and LLC halved) produced our strongest prefetcher overall at every cache size we tested: DuoArch-Nano. On the Fourth Data Prefetching Championship (DPC4) benchmarks with full-size caches, DuoArch-Nano delivers a 9.2% geomean IPC speedup (+10.5% on four-core mixes) while reducing four-core DRAM traffic by 11.4%, more than doubling the gains of the human champion BertiGO and the agentic ArchAgent v2. When the LLC is halved, DuoArch-Nano erases the baseline's 8.6% overall slowdown and edges out the full-LLC baseline overall (+0.88%), showing that agentic frameworks can generate prefetchers that reclaim megabytes of LLC SRAM per core with zero overall IPC penalty.
